groups.title: Setting out
groups.explanation: Each account begins with a boat journey. Read the different amounts of scene-setting.

groups.title: The storm and the appeal
groups.explanation: Notice how each account voices the disciples’ appeal.

groups.title: Calm, faith, and wonder
groups.explanation: Luke’s calming of the storm is already in verse 24 above. These are thematic reading groups, not exact sentence alignments.

notes.title: Notice the order
notes.text: In Matthew, Jesus questions the disciples before calming the storm (8:26). In Mark and Luke, the question about faith follows the calming (Mark 4:39–40; Luke 8:24–25). This is an observation about these passages; it does not by itself establish how they were composed.

notes.title: A question about understanding
notes.text: Dale B. Martin reads Mark’s disciples’ question about Jesus in 4:41 within a wider narrative pattern: the disciples struggle to understand him. This is Martin’s literary interpretation, not a claim that this scene independently establishes what the historical disciples knew.

citations.locator: Chapter 2, “A Historical Critical Reading of Mark” (begins 13:44); transcript discussion of Mark 4:41

notes.title: From comparison to interpretation
notes.text: Martin describes redaction criticism as studying how an author edits source material to communicate a message. That method depends on an argued account of the sources. Here, the alignment helps you notice the texts before choosing a theory about their relationship.

citations.locator: Chapter 5 (begins 35:44), explanation of redaction criticism; the lecture’s example is Matthew 14, a different sea episode

comparisons.title: The Lord’s Prayer
comparisons.subtitle: A shared prayer in two settings

groups.title: How Jesus introduces the prayer
groups.explanation: In Matthew, the prayer follows teaching about how to pray. In Luke, a disciple asks Jesus to teach the group to pray.

groups.title: The address and opening requests
groups.explanation: Both prayers address God as Father and ask for his name to be honored and his kingdom to come. Matthew also asks for God’s will to be done on earth as in heaven.

groups.title: Bread for the day
groups.explanation: Compare the timing of the request for bread. Matthew says “today” and Luke says “each day.”

groups.title: Forgiveness and temptation
groups.explanation: Both versions connect receiving forgiveness with forgiving others. Matthew closes with an additional request for deliverance from the evil one.

notes.title: Two settings for a shared prayer
notes.text: Matthew gives the prayer during the Sermon on the Mount. Luke introduces it with a disciple’s request after Jesus finishes praying. Read the verses before the prayer and notice how each Gospel gives the teaching a different introduction.

notes.title: How might the prayer have reached both Gospels?
notes.text: Mark Goodacre uses the Lord’s Prayer as an example of material shared by Matthew and Luke outside Mark. A common written source (Q) and Luke’s use of Matthew offer two possible explanations for that broader pattern. Olegs Andrejevs also examines a proposal that the prayer circulated in worship apart from Q. The two versions give us a place to test these explanations alongside other parallels.

readNext.label: The Lord’s Prayer in two copies of Luke

comparisons.title: The baptism of Jesus
comparisons.subtitle: Who is the voice speaking to?

groups.title: Jesus is baptized
groups.explanation: Matthew gives John and Jesus a brief exchange. Mark names John in a single verse. Luke places Jesus among the people being baptized and tells us he was praying when heaven opened.

groups.title: The Spirit descends and a voice speaks
groups.explanation: Read the voice’s first words in each Gospel. Who is being addressed?

notes.title: “This is” and “You are”
notes.text: In Matthew the voice says, “This is My beloved Son.” In Mark and Luke it speaks directly to Jesus, “You are My beloved Son.” A change of pronoun shifts the announcement from speaking about Jesus to speaking to him.

notes.title: Where does John fit in the story?
notes.text: Mark Goodacre sees Matthew and Luke addressing a question raised by Mark’s account. Why would Jesus receive a baptism that Mark has linked with repentance? Matthew gives John a chance to object and Jesus a reply. Luke reports John’s imprisonment just before the baptism scene and leaves the person who baptizes Jesus unnamed.

comparisons.title: Jesus heals a paralyzed man
comparisons.subtitle: From the crowded doorway to the dispute about forgiveness

groups.title: The man is brought to Jesus
groups.explanation: Start with how the man reaches Jesus. Each account then has Jesus notice the faith of the people who brought him and tell the man his sins are forgiven.

groups.title: Forgiveness is questioned
groups.explanation: Jesus responds to what his critics are thinking. Compare who objects and how Jesus replies in each account.

groups.title: The man gets up and goes home
groups.explanation: All three crowds glorify God. Notice what Matthew says God has given to human beings.

notes.title: Watch how the man reaches Jesus
notes.text: Mark says four people carry the man and make an opening in the roof. Luke describes the man being lowered through the roof tiles. Matthew moves straight from the man being brought on a mat to Jesus seeing the faith of those who brought him.

notes.title: What does the healing show?
notes.text: Judith König reads the dispute in Mark as a question about who has the authority to forgive sins. The man’s visible recovery shows what Jesus claims about his authority. Follow the order in Mark. When do the scribes object, and what does Jesus say the healing will show?

readNext.label: How can you tell who used whom?

comparisons.title: The Beatitudes
comparisons.subtitle: Blessings in Matthew and Luke, and the warnings that follow in Luke

groups.title: Where Jesus teaches
groups.explanation: Matthew places Jesus on a mountain. Luke sets the scene on a level place where people gather to hear Jesus and to be healed.

groups.title: Blessings in hardship
groups.explanation: These blessings are called the Beatitudes. Read the phrases about poverty, hunger, and grief in each Gospel and notice how their wording changes.

groups.title: Mercy, purity of heart, and peacemaking
groups.explanation: These three blessings are part of Matthew’s list. Luke’s blessing for people who are hated and rejected follows in the next group.

groups.title: Blessings for people who are mistreated
groups.explanation: Both accounts speak of a reward in heaven and recall what happened to the prophets. Notice how each Gospel describes the mistreatment.

groups.title: Luke’s warnings
groups.explanation: Luke follows his blessings with four warnings. Try matching each warning to an earlier blessing in Luke.

notes.title: How do the blessings address people?
notes.text: Matthew speaks of the “poor in spirit” and those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. In Luke, Jesus speaks to people who are poor and hungry now. Notice where Matthew shifts to addressing his listeners directly as “you.”

notes.title: A change in fortunes
notes.text: Mark A. Matson connects Luke’s blessings and warnings with Mary’s song earlier in the Gospel. Mary sings that God fills the hungry and sends the rich away empty. Read Luke’s blessings and warnings together and see whose circumstances are expected to change.

comparisons.title: The death of John the Baptist
comparisons.subtitle: What does Herod say when he hears about Jesus?

groups.title: Herod hears about Jesus
groups.explanation: In Matthew and Mark, Herod thinks Jesus is John raised from the dead. In Luke he acknowledges John’s execution and asks who Jesus could be. Luke closes the episode with Herod hoping to meet him.

groups.title: Why John is in prison
groups.explanation: Matthew and Mark now look back to John’s arrest. Notice who wants John dead and what holds that person back.

groups.title: A birthday promise
groups.explanation: Both accounts trace the request to Herodias, the girl’s mother. Mark lets readers hear the conversation between mother and daughter.

groups.title: Herod gives the order
groups.explanation: Herod’s guests have heard his promise. Follow the story through John’s burial and notice where each writer ends it.

notes.title: Who gets the news?
notes.text: Matthew begins with Herod hearing about Jesus. By the end, the news travels in the other direction. John’s disciples bury their teacher and go to tell Jesus what happened. Mark ends with the disciples laying John in a tomb.

notes.title: Why is Herod grieving?
notes.text: Mark says Herod had been protecting John. Matthew says Herod wanted John dead, yet he too grieves when the request comes. Mark Goodacre argues that Matthew kept the grief from Mark while changing Herod’s earlier motive. For Goodacre, this is one clue that Matthew used Mark’s account.

notes.title: What becomes of Herod’s question in Luke?
notes.text: Luke has already told readers how John came to be in prison. Here Herod mentions the execution and wants to see Jesus. Nathan L. Shedd connects that wish with a later scene. When Pilate sends Jesus to Herod, Luke says Herod has long hoped to see him perform a miracle.

readNext.label: How can you tell who used whom?

comparisons.title: Jesus is tempted in the wilderness
comparisons.subtitle: Which test comes last?

groups.title: Forty days in the wilderness
groups.explanation: The Spirit brings Jesus into the wilderness in all three accounts. Mark tells the whole episode in two verses, including the wild animals and the angels.

groups.title: The challenge about bread
groups.explanation: Matthew and Luke open the dialogue with Jesus hungry. Notice how the devil addresses him before mentioning bread.

groups.title: The temple and the kingdoms
groups.explanation: These two tests change places. Follow Matthew’s sequence and then Luke’s. Where does the devil take Jesus last in each account?

groups.title: The devil leaves
groups.explanation: Matthew closes with angels caring for Jesus, a detail Mark includes in the first group. Luke leaves open when the devil will return.

notes.title: Which reply gets the last word?
notes.text: Matthew puts the temple second and the mountain last. His final exchange is about worship. Luke puts the kingdoms second and the Jerusalem temple last. His final exchange is about whether to put God to the test.

notes.title: What does bread have to do with the wilderness?
notes.text: Jeannine K. Brown reads Matthew’s three replies from Deuteronomy as a link to Israel’s wilderness journey. Arland J. Hultgren traces the first reply in Luke to the same story. Moses recalls a time when the people went hungry and God fed them manna. Jesus answers the challenge about bread with words from that speech.

citations.locator: “Temptation One” and its context in Deuteronomy

comparisons.title: The women at the empty tomb
comparisons.subtitle: What do the women hear, and whom do they tell?

groups.title: The women arrive at the tomb
groups.explanation: Mark gives the women a question about the stone as they approach. Matthew describes an angel moving it. Luke begins with the women finding it already rolled away.

groups.title: The message at the tomb
groups.explanation: Look at who speaks to the women. Matthew describes an angel, Mark a young man dressed in white, and Luke two men in shining clothes.

groups.title: How the women respond
groups.explanation: Matthew’s women run to tell the disciples. Mark’s women flee in fear and silence. Luke tells readers how the apostles receive the women’s news.

groups.title: After the women leave
groups.explanation: Matthew follows the women as Jesus meets them on their way. Luke follows Peter as he runs to the tomb to look for himself.

notes.title: Listen for the name Galilee
notes.text: In Matthew and Mark, the disciples are to hear that they will see Jesus in Galilee. In Luke, the women are asked to remember what Jesus said while he was in Galilee. One place name points ahead to a meeting in two accounts and back to a conversation in the third.

notes.title: What makes the silence striking?
notes.text: Susan Miller sets the women’s silence beside an earlier scene in Mark. A woman Jesus has healed trembles and tells him what happened. At the tomb, women who stayed to watch the crucifixion are also trembling. This time fear keeps them from speaking.

notes.title: Why stop at Mark 16:8?
notes.text: H. A. G. Houghton identifies two fourth-century Greek copies of Mark, called Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, that end with the women leaving the tomb. This comparison follows that ending. Other copies continue with verses 9–20, where Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene.

comparisons.title: The mustard seed and the yeast
comparisons.subtitle: Two parables about the kingdom

groups.title: A seed takes root
groups.explanation: Where does the seed grow? Look for what the birds do once the plant is grown.

groups.title: What comes next?
groups.explanation: Leaven is a starter that makes dough rise. Look for a woman mixing it into flour.

notes.title: The Two-Source hypothesis
notes.text: Picture Matthew and Luke each reading Mark and a second, proposed source called Q. If Q paired the seed with the yeast, both writers could preserve that order independently. Look again at the planting. Matthew gives the man a field and Luke gives him a garden. How much of their wording would you feel able to reconstruct?

citations.locator: introduction, on reconstructing Q from Matthew and Luke

notes.title: The Farrer hypothesis
notes.text: Picture Luke reading both Mark and Matthew. The seed and the yeast are already neighbors in Matthew. Luke could keep them together while giving each a question about the kingdom of God. Compare Luke’s two opening questions with the way Mark introduces the seed.

citations.locator: pp. 55–56, 64–67, on Luke’s use and arrangement of Matthew
abstract, on applying the Farrer-Goulder hypothesis to these parables

notes.title: How does Crook weigh the evidence?
notes.text: Zeba Crook tested three proposals on these passages, including the Two-Gospel view that Mark used Matthew and Luke. He judged that the Two-Source explanation faced the fewest difficulties here. The pairing helps that explanation, but Luke could also have kept a pair he found in Matthew. Which detail besides the order would you want each account to explain?

comparisons.introduction: Which Gospels tell these two parables together? Read the passages, then try two explanations for the pairing.

comparisons.title: The mocking of Jesus
comparisons.subtitle: A minor agreement in the Passion narrative

groups.title: What do the mockers ask?
groups.explanation: Follow the words spoken to Jesus. Then look back to see which accounts mention a blindfold.

notes.title: Five words in common
notes.text: All three accounts include the command to prophesy. Matthew and Luke also give the mockers the same question, rendered “Who hit You?” in the BSB. Mark’s account moves directly from the command to further blows.

greek.gloss: Who is it that struck you?

notes.title: What makes this a minor agreement?
notes.text: Scholars use this term for a small point where Matthew and Luke agree with each other while differing from Mark inside a story that all three tell. On Austin Farrer’s proposal, Luke could draw on Mark for a scene and remember a detail from Matthew. This gives the shared question a possible route from one Gospel to the other.

citations.locator: pp. 60–62, on Matthew and Luke agreeing against Mark

notes.title: Could a copyist have brought the accounts closer?
notes.text: B. H. Streeter proposed that the question first stood in Luke and that an early copyist added it to Matthew. His proposal makes Matthew and Luke independent at the time of composition. The wording he proposed for Matthew is conjectural. The surviving copies he discusses already have the question.

citations.locator: chapter 11, discussion of Matthew 26:68 and Luke 22:64
